title: When a child dies
hook: the hardest grief; Christians hold it with Rachel weeping and with hope

segments.voice: Yesterday, growing old: cast me not off, until I have shewed thy strength. Your line was tell the next generation.

A small coffin is lighter than it should be. Nothing anyone says beside it makes it fit. This lesson goes slowly, and it's fine to stop at any point. If this is your grief, nothing here is meant to explain it away. The Bible doesn't either. It gives a mother's voice, weeping in a town called Ramah, a voice that refuses to be comforted. Christians have kept her voice in their scripture, and they hold this grief beside her.

Her name is Rachel. In Genesis she is the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and she dies on the road. Later, the prophet Jeremiah hears her again, weeping over her people as they are carried away. In the King James words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Refused to be comforted. The Bible doesn't scold her. It writes it down. Then Matthew's Gospel picks up the same line, after Herod has the little children of Bethlehem killed: "Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." Right inside the Christmas story, a mother who cannot be consoled. Then a second thing. In Jeremiah, God answers the weeping: "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD." And then, "there is hope in thine end." Weeping, then hope. Not hope instead of weeping. King David, when his infant son dies, says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me." Christian funeral prayers speak of the hope of the resurrection, and some Christians speak of seeing loved ones again. Churches describe that hope in different ways, and some leave the details with God. Both voices stay in the book. The tears are not a failure of faith. In the Bible, they are part of it.

If you know a mother or father who has lost a child, at any age, bring their face to mind; if not, hold the ones you'll never meet, in a hospital tonight or a town at war. Stay with them without reaching for words, the way someone sits beside a person who is crying, and if you pray, simply say Rachel's name and let God fill in the rest. If this grief is your own and it feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
When a child dies. The grief the Bible gives to Rachel, who would not be comforted, and the hope held beside it, without taking her tears away.
Your line: rachel weeping. Her tears stay in the book, beside the hope. Day one thousand four hundred three, done.

howItsDone: Christians mourn children with funerals, prayers and the hope of the resurrection; churches hold services of remembrance, some offer support groups for bereaved parents, and traditions differ in how they speak about children who die.

fork.setup: you're one of King David's servants. while his infant son was sick, David fasted and lay on the ground. now the child has died, and you're afraid to tell him. when he finds out, what does David do?
options: he tears his clothes and refuses food for many more days.
he gets up, washes, worships, and eats.
he blames his servants and sends them away.
fork.reveal: David rises, washes, goes to worship, then eats. his servants are confused, and he says: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me."

what a scholar hears: Matthew sets Jeremiah's lament right inside the Christmas story, so the birth of Jesus is told with Rachel's weeping next to it.

chat.says: My friend lost her baby. Does the Bible have anything for a grief like hers?
options: Yes. It gives Rachel, weeping for her children, a voice, and sets hope beside her tears.
Not really. Matthew keeps the Christmas story free of any grieving mothers at all.
A little. Rachel appears once, in Genesis, and the Bible never mentions her again.
chat.meaning: Jeremiah and Matthew both keep Rachel's weeping in scripture, and Jeremiah sets there is hope in thine end beside it, without taking her tears away.

Ramah.meaning: the town where Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping

Rahel.meaning: the King James spelling of Rachel in Jeremiah

Rachel.meaning: mother of Joseph and Benjamin in Genesis

Herod.meaning: the king who has Bethlehem's little children killed

notes: 'there is hope in thine end' (Jeremiah 31:17) is quoted in the voice; it is part of the cited range 31:16–17. Confirm KJV wording.
Matthew 2:16 has Herod kill the children of Bethlehem two years old and under; the script says little children and gives no age.

The hope of seeing children again is stated as a Christian hope, with 'churches speak of that hope in different ways'; Keeper may want to name traditions (e.g. teaching on infants who die unbaptized differs across churches) or keep it general for a grieving listener.
2 Samuel 12:23 is sometimes read as David going to the grave rather than reunion; the script lets it stand as David's own words.
Sensitive day: the hook invites the listener to stop at any point. Keeper to check tone for bereaved parents.
